description: How believers experience God: revelation, miracles, conversion and mystical experience.
content_html:
How Do Believers Think God Is Revealed?

Many religious believers do not arrive at their faith primarily through philosophical arguments. Instead, they claim direct or indirect experience of God. The idea that God makes himself known to human beings is called revelation. Christian theology traditionally distinguishes two kinds: general revelation (available to everyone, through creation and conscience) and special revelation (specific acts of God, such as scripture or the incarnation of Jesus Christ).

The opening of John’s Gospel (John 1:14) expresses the Christian conviction that God’s ultimate act of self-revelation was becoming human: “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.” This is the doctrine of the incarnation — that Jesus Christ is the Word of God made visible in human form. For Christians, knowing Jesus is the most direct way of knowing God.

Other means through which believers say God is revealed include: meeting inspirational people whose lives seem to embody divine goodness; encountering scripture; the voice of conscience; and God’s apparent action in history. In Islam, revelation came through the angel Jibril to the Prophet Muhammad, producing the Qur’an as the final and perfect word of Allah. Jewish believers point to the Torah as the revealed law given to Moses at Sinai.

Key Fact

Revelation takes many forms: through scripture (the Bible, Qur’an, Torah), through the person of Jesus Christ (“The Word became flesh” — John 1:14), through conscience, through creation, through miracles, and through personal religious experience. Together these constitute the “sources of wisdom and authority” that believers draw on.

Miracles

Miracles are events that seem to go beyond what natural causes can produce, and which believers attribute to divine action. The Gospels record many miracles attributed to Jesus: healing the sick, walking on water, feeding five thousand people, and most significantly, the resurrection. For Christians, miracles are signs that God is active in the world and that the natural order is not closed to divine intervention.

The philosopher David Hume argued that belief in miracles is almost never justified. He defined a miracle as a violation of a law of nature, and argued that the evidence in favour of the natural law will always be stronger than the testimony of those who claim to have witnessed a miracle. People are prone to exaggeration and superstition. However, believers respond that Hume’s argument presupposes naturalism — the view that only natural causes exist — and so begs the very question at issue. If God exists, miracles are entirely possible.

Believers argue that miracles, especially the resurrection of Jesus, are strong evidence for God’s existence and power. If the resurrection happened, it demonstrates a God who can act in history and who validated Jesus’s claims. Many point to unexplained healings at places of pilgrimage such as Lourdes as continuing evidence of miraculous divine action.

Non-believers argue that what appear to be miracles are more likely to be coincidences, natural events not yet understood by science, or wishful thinking by people in emotionally heightened states. Humanists reject miracles entirely — they see the natural universe as self-contained and believe that religious reports of miracles reflect deeply held cultural and psychological needs rather than actual supernatural events. For the 15-mark “Discuss” format, presenting both views fairly and then evaluating which is more compelling is essential.

Forms of Religious Experience

Many people claim to have had direct experience of God or the divine. Philosophers and theologians have identified several types of religious experience.

Conversion involves a dramatic change of belief or life direction in response to what the person perceives as a divine encounter. The most famous example in the Christian tradition is the conversion of Saul of Tarsus on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:1–6). Saul was a persecutor of early Christians when he reported being struck down by a blinding light and hearing the voice of Jesus. He was left blind for three days and emerged as Paul, one of the most influential figures in early Christianity. His conversion was sudden, unexpected and transformative — the hallmarks many see as confirming its divine origin.

Key Fact

Saul’s conversion (Acts 9:1–6) is the specification’s named example of a conversion experience. He heard the voice of Jesus saying, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” Examiners may ask you to describe this event and evaluate whether it constitutes evidence for God’s existence.

Mystical experience is a profound sense of union with God or ultimate reality. It is typically described as indescribable, overwhelming, and accompanied by deep peace or insight. The philosopher William James identified four features common to mystical experiences: they are noetic (they convey knowledge), they are transient (short-lived), they are passive (the person feels acted upon, not acting), and they are ineffable (impossible to fully put into words). Many Christian mystics — such as Teresa of Avila and Julian of Norwich — described such experiences.

Charismatic and ecstatic experience is associated with the gifts of the Holy Spirit described in the New Testament. In charismatic worship, believers may speak in tongues (glossolalia), prophesy, or experience intense emotion as they feel the Holy Spirit moving among them. This form of experience is common in Pentecostal churches and Charismatic Catholic movements.

Visions and the Sacraments

Visions are supernatural perceptions in which a person claims to see or hear God, Jesus, Mary or another spiritual figure. They may be experienced with the physical eyes or as vivid images in the mind. Biblical examples include Isaiah’s vision of God’s throne (Isaiah 6) and John’s Revelation. In the modern era, many Catholics report appearances of the Virgin Mary at sites such as Fatima and Lourdes.

For many Christians, God is also encountered through worship and the sacraments. The Mass or Holy Communion is considered by Catholics and many other Christians to be a moment of genuine encounter with the risen Christ. During the Eucharist, the ordinary — bread and wine — becomes a vehicle for the extraordinary: the presence of God. This sacramental understanding means that for millions of believers, religious experience is not reserved for dramatic visions or conversions; it is available in the regular acts of corporate worship.

Believers argue that the widespread, cross-cultural nature of religious experience — reported across all traditions, in all times and places — is strong evidence that it points to a genuine spiritual reality. They apply the “principle of credulity” (Richard Swinburne): if an experience seems real, we should take it at face value unless there is specific reason not to. The sheer number and consistency of reports makes it implausible that all are wishful thinking or delusion.

Non-believers argue that religious experiences can be explained psychologically (wish-fulfilment, grief, suggestion) or neurologically (temporal lobe activity, oxygen deprivation). Sigmund Freud argued that belief in God is a form of collective wish-fulfilment — humanity’s desire for a cosmic parent figure. The fact that people’s religious experiences are shaped by their own culture (a Christian sees Jesus; a Muslim encounters Allah; a Buddhist experiences nibbana) suggests the experiences reflect prior belief rather than objective reality.
exam_tip_html: On questions about religious experience, use the correct vocabulary precisely: “conversion” is a change of life direction (Acts 9 for Saul); “mystical experience” involves union with ultimate reality; “charismatic/ecstatic” involves the gifts of the Spirit including glossolalia; “visions” are supernatural perceptions of God or heavenly figures. A common student error is to treat all religious experience as one type. For the 15-mark “Discuss,” a strong response will give at least two types of religious experience, evaluate whether they constitute evidence for God’s existence (engaging the principle of credulity vs the psychological explanation), and reach a justified conclusion. SPaG matters — correct spelling of “glossolalia,” “mystical,” “charismatic,” “revelation” and “conscience” (not ‘concious’) is expected in the extended response.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Revelation is how God makes himself known: through scripture, conscience, creation, miracles and the person of Jesus Christ (“The Word became flesh” — John 1:14). Miracles are events believers attribute to direct divine action; Hume challenged these but believers argue his objection presupposes naturalism.
  • Religious experiences take several forms: conversion (Saul / Paul on the Damascus road — Acts 9:1–6), mystical experience (union with God, indescribable), charismatic/ecstatic (gifts of the Spirit, including glossolalia), and visions (supernatural perceptions). Many also encounter God through the Mass or Holy Communion.
  • Evaluating religious experience requires engagement with both religious and non-religious perspectives — the principle of credulity supports taking experiences at face value; psychological and neurological explanations challenge this. A strong exam answer engages both sides before reaching a justified conclusion.

practice_questions.text: State one way in which believers think God might be revealed to human beings.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: through scripture / the Word of God; through Jesus Christ; through conscience; through miracles; through creation; through the life of inspirational people; through religious experience / worship / sacraments. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happened to Saul on the road to Damascus, according to Acts 9.
practice_questions.marks: Saul was struck down by a blinding light (1 mark); he heard the voice of Jesus asking why he was persecuting him, and was left blind for three days before emerging as a follower of Christ (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three different forms of religious experience that believers might have.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per form accurately identified and briefly described: conversion (a dramatic change of belief and life direction in response to a perceived encounter with God); mystical experience (a profound, often indescribable sense of union or contact with God or ultimate reality); charismatic/ecstatic experience (gifts of the Holy Spirit, including glossolalia, prophecy or healing in worship); visions (seeing or hearing God, Jesus or a heavenly figure); sacramental experience (encountering God through the Eucharist / Mass). [3 marks — up to 3 correct forms]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why some Christians consider religious experience to be evidence for God's existence.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per reason): 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a source. Example responses: (1) The conversion of Saul (Acts 9:1–6) involved a dramatic, unexpected encounter with the risen Jesus that transformed a persecutor into an apostle; the radical change in his life is seen as evidence that the experience was genuine and divine in origin. (2) The principle of credulity (Swinburne): if an experience seems real, it should be taken at face value; the widespread, cross-cultural nature of religious experience makes coincidence or mass delusion implausible; John 1:14 grounds this in the Christian belief that God actively reveals himself in the world. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Religious experiences are the strongest evidence for the existence of God.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Religious experiences are reported across all cultures and historical periods, giving them cross-cultural weight; the conversion of Saul (Acts 9:1–6) involved life-transforming consequences — unlikely to be explained as wish-fulfilment. The principle of credulity supports taking such experiences seriously. Sacramental experience (Mass / Holy Communion) provides ongoing access to divine encounter for millions. Mystical experiences carry the marks of noetic value, transience, passivity and ineffability identified by William James, suggesting they involve genuine contact with something beyond the self.

Arguments against: Psychological explanations (Freud: wish-fulfilment; the desire for a cosmic parent) and neurological explanations (temporal lobe activity) offer natural accounts of religious experience without needing God. The culturally-conditioned nature of experiences (Christians see Jesus; Muslims encounter Allah) suggests experiences reflect prior belief rather than objective reality. David Hume's scepticism about miracles extends to religious experiences: testimony is always weaker than the evidence for natural law. Even if the experience is genuine, it does not logically prove the God of any specific religion exists.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named thinkers and sources; explicit weighing (e.g. the cultural-conditioning argument vs the cumulative weight argument); justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with some development and at least one source; conclusion present.
Developing: Both sides attempted but unevenly; limited sources; weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; few sources; little to no conclusion. [15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Mass or Holy Communion can be considered a form of religious experience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per way): 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a source. Example responses: (1) Catholics believe that during the Eucharist the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation) — this means every Mass is an encounter with the risen Jesus, making it a form of direct religious experience of God's presence; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26 grounds this in the words of Jesus at the Last Supper. (2) Even for Christians who do not hold transubstantiation, Communion is a sacramental act in which God's grace is understood to be genuinely communicated to believers; sharing bread and wine in the context of worship can produce feelings of peace, forgiveness and renewal that many describe in terms resembling mystical experience. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What is 'glossolalia' as described in the context of charismatic Christian worship?
options: The act of speaking in an unknown language as a gift of the Holy Spirit
A vision of the Virgin Mary

knowledge_checks.q: According to Acts 9:1–6, what happened to Saul on the road to Damascus?
options: He was baptised by Peter and received the Holy Spirit
He had a vision of heaven and heard angels singing
He was struck by a blinding light and heard the voice of Jesus
He read the scriptures and immediately believed

knowledge_checks.q: John 1:14 states that 'The _____ became flesh and made his dwelling among us', describing the incarnation of Jesus Christ.
A _____ experience involves a profound, often indescribable sense of union with God or ultimate reality, typically described as passive and transient.
Match each form of religious experience to its description:
right: A dramatic change of life direction in response to a perceived encounter with God
A profound, often indescribable sense of union with ultimate reality
A supernatural perception of God or a heavenly figure seen with the eyes or in the mind

flashcard_questions.q: What is revelation in religious belief?
flashcard_questions.a: The way God makes himself known to human beings, through creation, conscience, scripture or special acts like miracles.

flashcard_questions.q: What does John 1:14 say about how God is revealed?
flashcard_questions.a: 'The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us' — the incarnation of Jesus is God's ultimate self-revelation.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was Saul before his conversion, and what changed?
flashcard_questions.a: A persecutor of early Christians; after Acts 9 he became Paul, one of Christianity's most influential apostles.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to Saul on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:1–6)?
flashcard_questions.a: He was struck by a blinding light and heard Jesus's voice; he was blind for three days before his conversion.
A profound, often indescribable sense of union with God or ultimate reality, felt as passive, transient and noetic.
Speaking in tongues — an unknown language believed by charismatic Christians to be a gift of the Holy Spirit.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a charismatic experience and a mystical experience?
flashcard_questions.a: Charismatic involves gifts of the Spirit in worship (tongues, prophecy); mystical involves personal union with God, often alone.

flashcard_questions.q: What does conscience have to do with revelation?
flashcard_questions.a: Believers understand the inner sense of right and wrong as the voice of God guiding moral decision-making.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a 'miracle' in religious belief?
flashcard_questions.a: An event that appears to break natural laws and is attributed to direct divine action.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Hume's main argument against believing in miracles?
flashcard_questions.a: Evidence for a natural law always outweighs testimony claiming a violation of it.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Mass or Holy Communion, and why do some believers call it religious experience?
flashcard_questions.a: A sacrament in which bread and wine are shared; Catholics believe it is a genuine encounter with the risen Christ.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 'principle of credulity' in relation to religious experience?
flashcard_questions.a: If an experience seems real, it should be taken at face value unless there is specific reason not to (Swinburne).

glossary_terms.definition: The way in which God makes himself known to human beings, either through natural means (creation, conscience) or through special acts (scripture, miracles, the life of Jesus).
A term from John's Gospel identifying Jesus as the eternal creative power and reason of God, made flesh in the incarnation.
The inner sense of right and wrong that believers often understand as the voice of God guiding moral decision-making.
Events that appear to break the laws of nature and are attributed to the direct action of God.
A personal encounter or sense of the presence of God or the divine, which may take many forms including visions, inner voices, feelings of peace or dramatic transformations.
A deeply personal, often indescribable experience of union or direct contact with ultimate reality or God, typically involving feelings of peace, oneness and transcendence.
A form of Christian worship and religious experience associated with the Holy Spirit, often involving glossolalia (speaking in tongues), prophecy, healing or ecstatic emotional states.
The practice of speaking in an unknown language, believed by charismatic Christians to be a gift of the Holy Spirit.
Supernatural experiences in which a person perceives an image or message from God or a spiritual being, which may be seen with the eyes or in the mind.
The central act of Christian worship, also called Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper, in which bread and wine are shared in memory of, or in actual union with, Jesus Christ.
